about.heading: About
bio: For 6+ years at Prodigy Game, I developed and shipped features for a large-scale HTML5 application serving millions of monthly active users, working primarily in TypeScript, React, and PixiJS. That work ranged from rebuilding monetization and purchase flows (which lifted membership conversions by 20%) to building internal React tools that sped up how the whole team shipped features, to hunting down the performance and production bugs that only surface at real scale.

I care about clean, maintainable systems and measurable outcomes, including code that's fast, tested, and easy for the next person to build on. Because my background spans frontend web and game development, I'm comfortable with complex, real-time, highly interactive UI where performance is non-negotiable.
I have also shipped several of my own published games on the side.
I'm currently open to full-time Frontend / Web Developer roles, remote or in the Greater Toronto Area. If you're building something that needs to be fast, polished, and scalable, let's talk.

experience.title: Prodigy Education
experience.tagline: Web and mobile MMO teaching math and science to millions of students across North America.
experience.summary: Web and mobile MMO that teaches math and science to millions of students. Contributed across battle system, store infrastructure, premium currency, and IAP unification.
description: Prodigy is a live-service educational MMO used in schools across the US and Canada, gamifying math and science for grades 1 to 8. Jose worked across multiple feature teams (standard features, battle system, and monetization), shipping production code to a live audience of millions.

The game runs on a custom engine built on PixiJS with TypeScript, originally written in Phaser, giving the role unusually broad exposure to both game development patterns and web engineering practices. A monetization feature Jose owned directly contributed to measurable A/B test improvements.
highlights: Battle system revamp: laid the groundwork for a more engaging combat experience, reworking core architecture for extensibility
Tower Town: designed and implemented a focus-mode zone where players build and decorate their own town while answering more questions
Store revamp: part of the team that made the store more data-driven, added bundle support, and built React-based internal web tooling for content management
Premium currency (Magicoin): contributed to the introduction of the game's premium currency system
IAP unification: owned the client-side aspect of unifying in-app purchase systems across web and mobile
UI development: built numerous interface screens across different feature areas
Animations: implemented character and UI animations using Spine
features: Tower Town: A special zone that acts as focus time for players, where more questions are answered in average while the player builds and decorates their own little town
RPG Battle System: Was involved in the recent revamp of the battle system, laying foundations for a more engaging experience
Store: Was part of the team that revamped the store experience by making it more data driven and adding new features like bundles
Premium Currency: Was part of the team that introduced Magicoin, the premium currency of the game
IAP: Was in charge of the client-side aspect of IAP systems unification between web and mobile

credits.name: Jose Montenegro
credits.role: Software Developer (Standard Features, Battle System, Monetization)

experience.whatILearned: Working at Prodigy across battle, store, and monetization teams produced a developer who is comfortable with the full weight of live-service production: QA handoffs, cross-team coordination, product constraints, and shipping to a real audience where regressions have consequences. The web-native stack (PixiJS, TypeScript, React) meant game development patterns had to coexist with web engineering discipline, a combination that broadened technical range considerably.

experience.title: Illuminia Studios
experience.tagline: Gameplay programmer for BOAA, a fast-paced arcade game shipped on Android, iOS, and the Microsoft Store.
experience.summary: Gameplay programmer for BOAA, a fast-paced Afrofuturist arcade game shipped to Android, iOS, and the Microsoft Store. Built character controller, enemy AI, hazard systems, and multiplayer features.
description: At Illuminia Studios, I was the Gameplay Programmer for BOAA, a pick-up-and-play arcade game with an Afrofuturist aesthetic, released on Android, iOS, and the Microsoft Store. Version 0.4.0 included arcade mode, multiplayer, and leaderboards.

The studio was working toward a story mode and EOS blockchain integration for player collectibles before ceasing operations due to funding constraints. BOAA built a small dedicated community on the Microsoft Store before the shutdown.
highlights: Character controller: built the core player movement and feel for an arcade action game
Enemy design and implementation
Playing field hazards system
UI implementation across game screens
Shipped to three platforms: Android, iOS, and Microsoft Store
features: Pick-and-play arcade action
Fun art style and game world inspired by Afrofuturism
Multiplayer and Leaderboards
experience.whatILearned: Illuminia was the first startup experience with fast-paced development, direct trade-offs against deadlines, and the reality that a technically solid product can still be halted by funding rather than quality. It reinforced existing Unity expertise and introduced the practical discipline of shipping to multiple mobile storefronts simultaneously.

experience.title: Learn Safari
experience.tagline: Gameplay programmer for Spanish Safari, an educational game teaching Spanish to children aged 3 to 9.
experience.summary: Gameplay programmer on Spanish Safari, an educational Unity game teaching Spanish to children aged 3 to 9, shipped to iOS and web as v1.0.
description: At Learn Safari, I was a Gameplay Programmer on Spanish Safari: the company's primary product teaching Spanish to children aged 3 to 9 through a mix of 3D world exploration and 2D educational minigames. I was involved from early development through the 1.0 release in October 2016.

Built in Unity for iOS and web, the game uses a cartoony 3D overworld connecting to self-contained 2D minigames that reinforce language lessons. This was my first professional role in game development.
highlights: 3D navigation systems for player characters in the overworld
Internal inventory management system
Minigame development end-to-end: design, implementation, and integration with the main game loop
Multiple distinct 2D minigames, each targeting a specific language learning objective
Shipped to iOS and web as v1.0
features: Fun minigames that make it easy to learn
Cute world with friendly characters
Lessons are still being added to the game
3D navigation systems for the characters

hero.alt: Learn Safari Spanish Safari game screenshot

experience.whatILearned: Learn Safari was my first professional role in game development. It established the habits that I carry through all later work: estimating deliverables, collaborating within a team under production constraints, and building the kind of Unity debugging and optimization fluency that only comes from shipping real software. The minigame architecture of self-contained modules that interface cleanly with the main game became an early model for thinking about system boundaries.

projects.title: Drury Lane Damage
projects.tagline: Fight as the Muffin Man's monster in this baked beat-em-up
projects.summary: Fight as the Muffin Man's monster in this baked beat-em-up - Submission to NESJam 2026 using Godot 4.
description: Play as the Muffin Man's monster in a retro beat-em-up, defeating other cursed pastries. Built in 15 days for NESJam 2026 (theme: Horrible night to have a curse)

I was part of the programming team with 3 other programmers. My main role within this team was coding the UI, most of the in-game cutscenes, the prologue level, the dialogue sequences, the title/credits screens and the opening sequence
highlights: Used a smaller version of Akoya's node-based system for composable sequences when making cutscenes, where each sequence was a list of behavior nodes ran sequentially
The dialogue system was data-driven, with a textbox component that took dialogue data such as the voice audio to play and the list of individual dialogue pieces to run sequentially
Game text is able to accept wildcard text to replace depending on different conditions. For example, controls text would automatically change depending on the device used
features: Fight through the streets at night, defeating the Muffin Man's cursed pastries
Use punches and combos, as well as the blueberry projectile powerup
Retro-styled cinematic experience in the opening and ending scenes

jam.name: NESJam 2026
jam.theme: Horrible night to have a curse

credits.name: Robyn_cvh
credits.role: Programming, Writing, Music, Art, Font, VO

projects.whatILearned: Implementing the dialogue system taught me about the challenges in integrating sound with moving text, as well as timing the two together. The resulting system made in the jam period definitely has room for improvement, but it is a solid start that worked well in the final product. Re-using the architectural form of Akoya's node based system for cutscene exposed a weakness in it: since it has to use scene nodes, it can be prone to usability issues when including references to things outside the root of the sequence. This can be mitigated with more careful scene architecture or by transforming the system into a truly data-driven one where all the configuration lives on a single object

projects.title: Akoya and the Lost Pearl
projects.tagline: A mermaid magical girl Metroidvania. 7th place out of 80 jam entries.
projects.summary: A mermaid magical girl Metroidvania built for Metroidvania Month Jam 31. Placed 7th out of 80 entries.
description: Akoya is a mermaid who transforms between land and sea forms to navigate a sunlit beach and its dark underwater caves. Built in a month for Metroidvania Month Jam 31 (theme: Magical Girls), it placed 7th out of 80 entries.

I handled all programming and level design for a four-person team, architecting the state machine, FMOD audio integration, a custom water shader, and the dual-environment movement system that makes the transformation feel mechanically distinct rather than cosmetic.
highlights: Node-based state machine used across the player character, all enemies, and interactables. New behaviors could be added mid-jam without touching unrelated code
Dual-environment movement: grounded combat mode and six-directional swim mode, each with separate physics, animation states, and hitbox behavior
FMOD integration via the Godot FMOD extension, with real-time crossfading between above-water and underwater soundscapes
Custom GLSL water shader
Level maps initially authored in Tiled, then migrated to Godot's native tilemap editor mid-project for better tooling in the final design stretch
features: Transform into a mermaid to swim underwater
Fight against crabs, bats, and an evil mermaid
Explore a gorgeous beach and dark caves

hero.alt: Akoya and the Lost Pearl: mermaid protagonist navigating the beach

screenshots.alt: Akoya and the Lost Pearl: screenshot 1
Akoya and the Lost Pearl: screenshot 2

projects.whatILearned: Keeping state machine transitions explicit and data-driven paid off immediately when a new enemy type was needed two days before the deadline. FMOD is powerful but its Godot support was limited enough to block a web build entirely, which is worth factoring in early. Mid-jam tool migrations are a real risk: the Tiled-to-Godot switch was the right long-term call, but it should be a deliberate day-one task rather than absorbed as scope creep. The water shader was a first step into GLSL as there is more to build on there.

projects.title: ForgeFront
projects.tagline: Autobattler RTS with roguelite elements. Destroy the Anomalous Hives across space and time.
projects.summary: Autobattler RTS with roguelite elements built for Brackeys Jam 2026.1. Placed 613th out of 1427 entries.
description: ForgeFront blends autobattler, RTS, and roguelite mechanics. Set your factory build order, farm minerals, and push through procedurally generated maps. Between runs, minerals convert to chips that buy permanent upgrades.

Built in one week for Brackeys Jam 2026.1 by a large coordinated team of 16 credited contributors spanning directors, developers, artists, musicians, and SFX designers. Placed 613th out of 1427 entries. I contributed as one of five developers, implementing the in-run and persistent upgrades system, doing some of the bot behaviors, fixing UI bugs, implementing bot sfx and working through the integration challenges that come with a team this size under a one-week constraint.
highlights: In-run upgrade systems and permanent chip-based progression between runs
Procedurally generated maps supporting the roguelite run structure
Systems-heavy architecture designed so five developers could contribute in parallel
Cross-functional coordination across developers, directors, artists, and SFX under a one-week deadline
features: RTS and Autobattler combination
Roguelike runs coupled with permanent upgrades
projects.whatILearned: Managing a large team under a one-week deadline is primarily a systems design problem: the game needs to be architected so that everyone can contribute in parallel without constant integration pain. The main lesson was that upfront system planning pays off disproportionately at this scale. Time invested on day one saves multiples later. The second half of the project was largely integration work, and the clearest takeaway is that more deliberate planning at the start would have made that phase significantly smoother. On the other hand, I was able to code a roguelike upgrade system that worked in a run-only setting as well as persistently, which was a great learning experience.

projects.title: VIZARD
projects.tagline: A hacker-themed mystery game. Uncover a company's secrets through a Linux-style terminal.
projects.summary: A hacker-themed mystery game built for Global Game Jam 2026, now in continued development. Uncover a company's secrets through a Linux-style terminal.
description: VIZARD is a mystery game inspired by S.P.L.I.T. and The Rootrees are Dead. You play a hacker-for-hire tasked with exposing a mysterious company by connecting to employee workstations, reading private files, and piecing together the truth from internal chats and documents.

First built in one week for Global Game Jam 2026, the game is now in continued post-jam development. The central interface is a faithful Linux-style console the player uses to navigate the company's network. I served as both lead programmer and primary designer, writing the puzzles and dialogue while building the data-driven architecture that underlies the terminal.
highlights: Data-driven terminal system: console commands, file system, employee profiles, and chat logs are all defined in data - adding new content requires no code changes
Localization pipeline using Unity's table system connected to an external Google Sheet for content management
Ongoing post-jam development expanding the design and asset management systems
features: Faithful simulation of a Linux-style console with many familiar commands
Awesome retro aesthetic in a modern world
Intriguing story that promises more than what initially seems
projects.whatILearned: This was the first project where design ownership was the primary creative responsibility. The data-driven architecture meant the terminal could be extended without touching code, which proved valuable when scope grew post-jam. Working on localization via Unity's table and Google Sheet pipeline added a practical production skill that carries into larger projects.

projects.title: Dragon Warrior NES Clone
projects.tagline: A faithful 1-to-1 clone of Dragon Warrior I for the NES, built in Godot for fun and practice.
projects.summary: A faithful 1-to-1 clone of Dragon Warrior I for the NES, built solo in Godot 4 for fun and practice.
description: A near-complete recreation of Dragon Warrior I (Dragon Quest in Japan) built solo in Godot 4 over roughly a month. The only addition beyond the original is a debug menu with cheats and skips for development convenience.

The focus was on faithful reproduction: the turn-based battle system, overworld navigation, shop and inn interactions, save files, and the 8-bit visual effects (fade transitions, UI flicker) that define the NES era aesthetic. Playable directly in the browser with no download required.
highlights: Battle system built on an MVC architecture. View updates the model through controller commands and the model returns a list of battle events for the view to consume. Designed to scale to more complex turn-based systems or a client-server setup
8-bit era shaders and UI effects: full-screen fadeout, text rendering, and period-accurate visual behavior
Progress saving on WebGL via browser local storage
Debug menu with cheats and skips not present in the original
features: Full recreation of overworld, towns, dungeons, shops, inns, and the complete quest structure

hero.alt: Dragon Warrior NES Clone: overworld view

projects.whatILearned: The MVC pattern for turn-based systems was the key engineering insight here: the view sends commands to the controller, the controller updates the model, and the model emits a flat list of battle events for the view to replay in sequence. This decoupling makes the system straightforward to extend and naturally supports a client-server split if needed. Writing 8-bit era shaders and UI code was a satisfying exercise in deliberate platform constraints.

projects.title: Cursed Ruby
projects.tagline: A Castlevania-flavored Metroidvania built solo. 6th place out of 82 jam entries.
projects.summary: A Castlevania-flavored Metroidvania built solo for Metroidvania Month Jam 17. Placed 6th out of 82 entries.
description: Ruby is cursed and on a deadline. She has weeks to storm her enemy's gothic castle and break the hex before it kills her. Cursed Ruby is a Castlevania-inspired Metroidvania built entirely solo for Metroidvania Month Jam 17, where it placed 6th out of 82 entries.

As the sole programmer, I owned every system: movement, enemy AI, progression gating, save state, UI, and audio wiring while coordinating freelance contributors across art, music, SFX, and voice on a jam schedule. The state machine and core systems built here became the direct foundation for Akoya and the Lost Pearl, surviving the transition to Godot 4.
highlights: Reusable state machine and physics architecture carried forward into future projects
Tilemap-based level system with ability-gated progression
Progression save system
WebGL build target alongside Windows
features: Castlevania-inspired enemies and environments, courtesy of Ansimuz
Wall-sticking spear ability: fires into walls and stays there, becoming a temporary platform that creates puzzle-platformer moments inside an action game
Localized air dash: momentum-independent aerial burst that functions as precise repositioning rather than room-crossing flight

credits.name: Nyebe
credits.role: Title screen, game over, and intro art

hero.alt: Cursed Ruby: protagonist Ruby in the gothic castle environment

videos.alt: Cursed Ruby: air dash ability showcase

projects.whatILearned: This project is where Godot became a genuine tool rather than an experiment. State machines, physics, tilemaps and more settled into reusable patterns that survived the engine upgrade to Godot 4. Designing unconventional abilities led to level design challenges where I needed to provide compelling uses as well as making the abilities easy to understand. Moves that felt obvious to me as the programmer were invisible to fresh players until the environment forced experimentation.

projects.title: Jumping Jack
projects.tagline: A faithful Windows remake of the classic Jumping Jack ZX Spectrum arcade game.
projects.summary: A faithful Windows remake of the classic Jumping Jack ZX Spectrum arcade game, built as a reverse-engineering exercise.
description: A remake of Jumping Jack, the 1983 ZX Spectrum arcade game originally published by Imagine Software. The original's challenge is preserved intact: navigate upward through rows of platforms, clear gaps with precise jumps, and avoid enemies with deliberately minimal controls (arrow keys to move and jump, Enter to start).
The project began as a personal exercise in extracting the design of a classic game through reverse engineering and reproducing it faithfully. Available on itch.io as a free Windows download.
highlights: Minimal, intentional control scheme matching the original (arrow keys + Enter)
Reverse-engineered design from playing the original
features: Faithful recreation of the Jumping Jack ZX Spectrum arcade game, including the small lore between levels
projects.whatILearned: Remaking a classic is a useful design exercise precisely because you cannot take shortcuts: every mechanic has to be understood well enough to reproduce it accurately. Reverse-engineering how the original handled platform rows, enemy movement, and gap detection built an intuition for classic arcade design principles that is harder to acquire from reading about them.

projects.title: Princess Showdown
projects.tagline: A 2D Unity platformer for IGMC 2018. Switch between two magic forms to escape a rival's dungeon.
projects.summary: A 2D Unity platformer for IGMC 2018. Placed 43rd out of 281 in the People's Choice Vote.
description: Princess Showdown is a 2D platformer submitted to the Indie Game Making Contest 2018, built solo in Unity. Princess Rose has been thrown into her rival Serena's dungeon and must fight her way back to reclaim her crown. The core mechanic is a dual magic form system: players switch between two distinct modes to handle different enemy types and platforming hazards, with roughly 30 minutes of content from entry to crown.

It placed 43rd out of 281 in the People's Choice Vote. Keyboard and gamepad are both supported, with gamepad recommended. I published a Prototype Postmortem devlog after release, reflecting on what worked and what did not.
highlights: Two switchable magic forms that change combat approach and traversal options
Skeletal 2D animation for the player character
Virtual cameras and parallax backgrounds for environmental depth
Event sequencing system for in-gameplay cutscenes
Prototype Postmortem devlog published post-release
features: Enemy encounters and environmental hazards
Approximately 30 minutes of gameplay
Keyboard and gamepad support (gamepad recommended)

hero.alt: Princess Showdown: Princess Rose in combat

projects.whatILearned: This project introduced several technical challenges tackled for the first time: skeletal 2D animation, virtual cameras, parallax backgrounds, and event sequencing for cutscenes that occur mid-gameplay. The on-the-fly ability switching also required careful state management to keep transitions clean and responsive. Writing a public postmortem after release added a layer of reflection that sharpened the ability to assess design decisions critically.

projects.title: Dinosaur Rain
projects.tagline: A frantic dinosaur invasion action game built for GBCJAM #11 in a single day.
projects.summary: A frantic dinosaur invasion action game built for GBCJAM #11 in a single day. Theme: Frantic.
description: Dinosaur Rain is an action game built for GBCJAM #11, a game jam for Game Development students at George Brown College. The jam's theme was "Frantic," and the game delivers on it directly: dinosaurs rain from the sky and players must survive the onslaught.

Built in Unity by a three-person team in a single day, the result demonstrates solid scope judgment - a simple, focused premise that was achievable under a one-day constraint and communicates the theme without ambiguity. Playable in the browser or downloadable for Windows.
highlights: Jam theme "Frantic" directly expressed through high-density dinosaur spawning and survival pressure
Completed in a single day by a three-person student team
Browser-playable via HTML5 and downloadable Windows build
features: Frantic action gameplay centered on a dinosaur invasion theme
Browser-playable via HTML5
Downloadable Windows build

hero.alt: Dinosaur Rain: dinosaurs raining from the sky

projects.whatILearned: A one-day jam demands a design that can be finished in one day. The main skill on display here is scope judgment: identifying a premise simple enough to build completely under the constraint, while still being coherent and fun. The team hit that target, which is the whole point of a short jam.

projects.title: Simple QBert
projects.tagline: A browser-playable Unity recreation of Q*bert's first level. Built as a class project in two days, which led directly to a professional role.
projects.summary: A browser-playable Unity recreation of Q*bert's first level, built as a class project in two days. Led directly to a professional role at Illuminia Studios.
description: Simple QBert recreates the first level of Q*bert, the 1982 Gottlieb arcade classic. The original is a puzzle-action game where the player hops across an isometric pyramid of cubes, changing their colors while avoiding enemies.

This was developed as a class assignment with a two-week window. It was completed in two days. That speed and fidelity led directly to a recommendation from the teacher, which landed me a position at Illuminia Studios. Playable free in the browser, no download needed.
highlights: Local Leaderboards
Recreated enemy behavior and color-change puzzle mechanic from the 1982 original
Completed in 2 days against a 2-week class deadline
features: Browser-playable clone of Q*bert's first level
Faithful reproduction of the cult classic arcade puzzle-action gameplay
No download required - runs directly in the browser
projects.whatILearned: Reverse-engineering a classic game forces you to understand its systems at a fundamental level. The isometric cube-hopping, enemy routing, and color state logic all had to be understood precisely to reproduce them correctly. Finishing well ahead of schedule demonstrated that thorough problem decomposition matters more than time budgeted, and the professional opportunity that followed reinforced that publicly sharing quality work opens doors.

projects.title: Hands Off
projects.tagline: An uncomfortable hand-scratching action/shooter. Built in one day for GBCJAM #9 at George Brown College.
projects.summary: An uncomfortable hand-scratching action/shooter built in one day for GBCJAM #9. Theme: Uncomfortable.
description: Hands Off is an action/shooter created for GBCJAM #9 at George Brown College, where I studied Game Programming. The jam theme was "Uncomfortable," and the game commits fully to that: the mechanic is built around pushing away hands that are scratching a blackboard
Built by a two-person team in a single day. Playable directly in the browser via HTML5.
highlights: Completed in a single day by a two-person team
Browser-playable via HTML5
features: Action/shooter gameplay with an unconventional hand-scratching premise
projects.whatILearned: This was the first game jam experience at George Brown College. I learned that a simple, clearly scoped game can be built and shipped in one day if the design is disciplined from the start. Getting something complete and playable under that constraint is the whole goal.

projects.title: Chicken Feud
projects.tagline: A local two-player puzzle game for the Venezuela Duel Jam. Rescue a princess or tempt the hero with roasted chicken.
projects.summary: A local two-player puzzle game for the Venezuela Duel Jam. Asymmetric: one player rescues a princess, the other tempts the hero with roasted chicken.
description: Chicken Feud is a local multiplayer puzzle game made for the Venezuela Duel Jam. It was heavily inspired by Tetris Attack on the SNES. Sir Areponcio is on his way to rescue the princess, but an evil sorcerer keeps placing irresistible roasted chicken in his path. One player is the princess, pulling the hero forward. The other is the sorcerer, derailing him with temptation.

Two players, same machine, presented in Spanish. The technical challenge was creating a puzzle interface that worked at any screen resolution, with competing player goals legible simultaneously on one display. Playable in the browser.
highlights: Local multiplayer: one player pursues rescue, the other plays saboteur
Puzzle interface built to scale cleanly across screen resolutions
Browser-playable via HTML5
features: Design inspired by Tetris Attack
Local two-player competitive puzzle gameplay on the same machine
Quirky chicken-themed narrative and humor
projects.whatILearned: The design was heavily inspired by Tetris Attack, which meant studying how that kind of grid-based interface is constructed before building it. The most technically satisfying outcome was a resolution-independent puzzle layout which is a non-trivial UI engineering problem when the grid has to feel tight and precise.

projects.title: Stink Bomb Revenge
projects.tagline: A browser-based Unity puzzle prototype built on-site over three days at Global Game Jam 2015.
projects.summary: A browser-based Unity puzzle prototype built on-site over three days at Global Game Jam 2015.
description: Stink Bomb Revenge is a puzzle-survival prototype inspired by WarioWare and playable directly in the browser. A bully has stumbled into a stinky trap, and the player must figure out the bomb's logic and survive as long as possible before it triggers. The game layers puzzle-solving with a time-pressure survival challenge, requiring players to read and respond to the trap's mechanics under increasing urgency.
It was built by an 8-person team working on-site for three straight days at the Global Game Jam 2015, my first game jam experience. Built in Unity, compiled to HTML5.
highlights: Collaborative combination of mini-games coded by different developers integrated into one experience
Browser-playable via WebGL
Completed on-site over three consecutive days at Global Game Jam 2015
features: Browser-playable with no download required
Timed survival challenge against the bomb's mechanisms
Prototype-level scope with focused design

hero.alt: Stink Bomb Revenge: puzzle bomb interface

projects.whatILearned: This was the first game jam experience. Working on-site with a team for three straight days under a hard deadline is a different discipline from solo or remote development. Communication is king, integration problems surface faster, and shipping something coherent requires constant alignment. The experience established the fundamentals of jam-paced teamwork that I carried into every subsequent jam.

projects.title: So Club
projects.tagline: A media club app for organizing what a group watches, reads, and plays together.
projects.summary: Full-stack Next.js app for running media clubs: role-based groups, invite links, TMDB-powered search, and a shared backlog. Built solo and deployed to production.
description: So Club is a book club for every kind of media. Groups sign up, invite friends with a link, search for titles, and build a shared backlog they work through together. Movies are the first supported medium; books and games are planned against the same abstraction.

The whole stack is mine: Next.js App Router with server-side data fetching, Prisma over PostgreSQL on Supabase, Auth.js for database-backed sessions, and shadcn/ui on TailwindCSS for the interface. It runs in production on Vercel at so-club.com.
highlights: Pluggable media providers behind a MediaProvider interface (search + getByExternalId) returning a NormalizedMediaItem, so books and games can drop in beside TMDB without touching the group or backlog code
Normalized snapshots of each item are written to the database once it is added to a group, cutting repeat calls out to external APIs

Role-based authorization guards on every group-scoped page and server action: unauthorized requests redirect to sign-in, and non-members hitting a group URL directly get a 404 rather than a hint that the group exists
Three sign-in paths on one page: GitHub OAuth, Google OAuth, and passwordless email magic links via Resend, all on database-backed Auth.js sessions
Docker Compose Postgres plus a seed script that prints a ready-made invite link, so a fresh clone lands in a populated club
features: Groups with owner, admin, and member roles gating every action
Shareable invite links generated by group owners
Server-side movie search powered by the TMDB API
Shared group backlog that records which member added each title

screenshots.alt: So Club: sign-in with GitHub, Google, or an email magic link

projects.whatILearned:
The interesting design problem was making the app generic over media types without over-abstracting it before a second provider existed. Putting a narrow MediaProvider interface in front of TMDB, and normalizing everything to a shared shape with a per-medium metadata field, keeps the group and backlog layers unaware of where a title came from.

The authorization work was the other half. Instead of scattering permission checks, every group-scoped page and server action runs the same role guard, and it deliberately distinguishes needing to sign in from the resource not existing for you, so a private group's existence never leaks through the response.

projects.title: Movie Watchlist
projects.tagline: Search a movie database and keep a personal watchlist that persists in the browser.
projects.summary: Vanilla JavaScript app that searches TMDB and stores a personal watchlist in local storage. No framework, no backend.
description: A two-page app for finding films and saving them for later. Search hits the TMDB API and renders results with poster, runtime, genres, rating, and synopsis; one click moves a title onto the watchlist page, where it can be removed again.
Built with no framework and no backend: plain JavaScript, HTML, and CSS, with the watchlist held in browser local storage so it survives a reload.
highlights: TMDB search with results rendered from the API response: poster, runtime, genre list, rating, and synopsis
Watchlist persisted to browser local storage and shared between the search and watchlist pages with no backend
Written without a framework, so DOM rendering and state handling are done directly
features: Movie search against the TMDB database
Add and remove titles from a personal watchlist

projects.title: Color Scheme Generator
projects.tagline: Pick a seed color and a harmony rule, get a five-swatch palette back with its hex codes.
projects.summary: React and TypeScript practice project that generates color schemes from The Color API, with eight harmony modes and the hex codes shown for every swatch.
description: A small tool for generating palettes: choose a base color, choose one of eight harmony rules (monochrome, analogic, complement, triad, quad, and variants), and the app requests a matching five-color scheme from The Color API and renders it as full-height swatches with their hex codes.
Written as a React and TypeScript practice project on Vite, deliberately kept to a single focused interaction.
highlights: Eight harmony modes driven by The Color API scheme endpoint, from a single seed color and a mode selection
Typed API response handling in TypeScript, with the rendered swatches derived directly from the fetched scheme
Built on Vite and deployed as a static bundle to GitHub Pages
features: Native color picker for the seed color
Eight scheme modes: monochrome, monochrome dark and light, analogic, complement, analogic-complement, triad, and quad
Five-swatch output with hex codes shown under each color

hero.alt: Color Scheme Generator: an analogic scheme generated from a blue seed color

projects.whatILearned: A deliberately small React project to get the fundamentals clean: typing an external API response properly, keeping the fetched scheme as the single source of truth for what gets rendered, and shipping a Vite build to static hosting.
